hero.text: Games chosen for what each grade is actually learning, not a list that could belong to any class. Every one works with no equipment and forty-five pupils.

blocks.heading: Why these are arranged by grade
text: Most collections of classroom games are arranged by skill or by level, which leaves the teacher to work out whether a game fits the class in front of them. That is the hardest part, and it is the part usually left out.

These are arranged by grade instead, and each game is tied to language that grade is genuinely working on - so a Grade 7 game practises the past simple because Grade 7 is learning the past simple, and a Grade 10 game practises the kind of writing the Ordinary Level paper will ask for.

items.title: Grade 1
text: Listening, repeating and doing - colours, numbers, animals, classroom things, and following an instruction in English.

items.title: Grade 2
text: Short sentences instead of single words - plurals, this and that, family, the body, and simple questions.

items.title: Grade 3
text: Can and can't, where things are, days and weather, likes and dislikes, and the first written sentences.

items.title: Grade 4
text: The past simple, comparing two things, describing a person or a room, and telling somebody what you did.

items.title: Grade 5
text: Reading closely, putting sentences in order, giving reasons, and writing three or four connected sentences.

items.title: Grade 6
text: Introductions, the present simple and continuous, asking questions, and describing what is in front of you.

items.title: Grade 7
text: Telling what happened - the past simple and continuous, adverbs, giving instructions, and talking about the future.

items.title: Grade 8
text: The present perfect, reporting what somebody said, superlatives, and writing a short notice or message.

items.title: Grade 9
text: Conditionals, the passive, and the difference between formal and friendly English.

items.title: Grade 10
text: The writing formats the O/L paper asks for - notices, letters, dialogues, forms - done fast and to a word limit.

items.title: Grade 11
text: The O/L paper itself - each section done against a clock, marked against the criteria, and repaired.

blocks.heading: The four things that decide whether a game teaches anything
text: A game that goes well is not the same as a game that taught something. These four decide which you get, and none of them is about the game itself.
bullets: **Every pupil must produce language, not watch somebody produce it.** A quiz where one pupil answers and forty-four listen is a quiz with an audience. Teams that all write, all say the sentence, or all stand up are the difference.
**The rule must force the target language out.** If a pupil can win by pointing or by saying one word, they will. The language you want has to be the only way to score.
**Stop it early.** A game stopped while the class still wants it can be used again next week. A game played until it dies cannot be used again at all.

**Decide about mistakes before you start.** Correct everything and the game stops being a game; correct nothing and it stops being a lesson. Most teachers note two or three errors and deal with them at the end, on the board, with no names.

blocks.heading: Running a game in a class of forty-five
text: The commonest reason a teacher gives up on games is not the game. It is the four minutes of noise getting into teams and the four minutes getting back out, in a period of forty.
bullets: **Use the rows you already have.** Teams by row need no movement at all, and a class of forty-five is usually five or six teams without a single chair being shifted.
**One sheet per row, passed along.** It stops the confident pupil writing everything, and it needs no group work training.
**Give the instructions before the teams,** never after. Once a class is in teams it cannot hear you.
**Have a stopping signal the class already knows** and practise it once when nothing is at stake. A hand up, a clap pattern, anything - but the same one every time.
**Write the score where everybody can see it.** Half the discipline problems in a class game are disputes about the score.

pages.title: Grade 1 English Classroom Games
pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 1, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 1 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: listening, repeating and doing - colours, numbers, animals, classroom things, and following an instruction in English.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 1 class needs from a game
text: Grade 1 English is oral. The pupils are listening, repeating and doing, and they are not yet reading or writing in English, so none of these games asks a pupil to write anything.

What a game has to achieve at this age is narrower than it looks: every child says the word aloud, and every child understands an instruction given in English. Those two things are the whole lesson, and a game is simply the only way to get forty-five six-year-olds to do them forty times without complaining.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: Touch the colour
blocks.language: Colours, and the instruction *touch*
steps: Say *touch something blue*. Every pupil touches something blue within reach - a shirt, a bag, a friend's ribbon.
Look around and name what you see: *Kavindu is touching a blue bag. Good.* The class hears the colour again in a sentence.
Repeat with four or five colours, faster each time.
Finish with a colour that is hard to find, such as *touch something black*, and let them look around the room for it.
blocks.variation: Harder: two things at once - *touch something blue and something white.*
blocks.bigClass: This is better in a large class than a small one, because nobody moves from their place. Stand at the back for one round so the pupils at the back are the ones you can see.

blocks.name: The sound basket
blocks.language: Initial sounds, and any known nouns
steps: Say *I am putting things in my basket that begin with /b/.* Say three: *ball, book, bag.*
Ask the class for more. Accept any word beginning with the sound, and repeat each one back clearly so the whole class hears it correctly.
When a pupil offers a word with the wrong sound, do not say wrong. Say the word, then say the sound it starts with, then ask the class whether it goes in the basket.
Change the sound and split the class in two halves, each half finding words for a different sound.
blocks.variation: Easier: hold up or point to real objects in the room instead of asking them to think of words.
blocks.bigClass: Two halves rather than teams by row, because the counting is slow at this age and two groups is enough competition for six-year-olds.

blocks.name: Clap when you hear it
blocks.language: One target word or sound, heard inside a list
steps: Choose a word the class has just learned, for example *cat*.
Say a slow list of words, some of which are *cat*: *bag, cat, cup, cat, cake, cat.* The class claps once every time they hear it.
Start slowly. Speed up only when everybody is getting it.
Then swap the target word and do it again, and let a pupil read out the list - which at this age means saying words they know, not reading from paper.
blocks.variation: Harder: two target words with two different actions, clap for one and stand for the other.
blocks.bigClass: Perfect for a large class: forty-five pupils clapping together tells you instantly who is following and who is copying their neighbour half a second late.

blocks.name: Big voice, small voice
blocks.language: Any new word set - animals, food, classroom things
steps: Say a new word in a big voice. The class says it back in a big voice.
Say it in a small voice, almost a whisper. The class whispers it back.
Alternate unpredictably - big, small, small, big - so that they must listen rather than chant automatically.
Move through six or seven words this way, and end with the whole list in a whisper, which is the quietest the class will be all period.
blocks.variation: Add a slow voice and a fast voice, which practises the word's syllables without ever mentioning the word syllable.
blocks.bigClass: The volume change is the classroom management: a class that has just whispered a word is already quiet, so put this immediately before something that needs their attention.

blocks.name: Point to it first
blocks.language: Classroom objects: door, window, board, desk, bag, book, pen
steps: Name the objects with the whole class twice, pointing at each.
Put the pupils in pairs with their partner next to them - no movement.
Say an object. In each pair, the first of the two to point at it correctly wins that round. They keep their own score on their fingers.
After eight or nine objects, ask who has three fingers up, four, five. Everybody has a number, so nobody has lost.
blocks.variation: Harder: say a short sentence instead of a word - *the thing we write on* - so they must understand rather than recognise.
blocks.bigClass: Finger scoring is what makes this work with forty-five: no board, no paper, no dispute, and you can see every score from the front in one glance.

blocks.name: Count and stop
blocks.language: Numbers 1 to 20
steps: The class counts aloud together from one. You clap once, and they stop instantly on that number.
Say the number they stopped on, then start again from one.
Now go round the rows: the first pupil says *one*, the next *two*, and so on along the row and into the next. When you clap, the pupil whose turn it is sits down and the count starts again at one.
Keep it quick. The point is the counting, not the elimination.
blocks.variation: Harder: count backwards from twenty, or count in twos.
blocks.bigClass: Going along rows means every pupil says a number within two minutes, which individual questioning could never manage in a class of forty-five.

blocks.name: The animal walk
blocks.grouping: Whole class, standing at their places
blocks.language: Animals, and the verbs *walk, jump, fly, swim, run*
steps: Teach or revise five animals and the way each one moves: *a frog jumps, a bird flies, a fish swims.*
Everybody stands at their place. Say an animal; the class does the movement on the spot and says the verb: *jump!*
Then say a verb and let them call out an animal that does it.
Finish by saying an animal name quietly and letting the class move quietly, which brings the noise down before they sit.
blocks.variation: Ask one confident pupil to be the caller for the last three rounds.
blocks.bigClass: On the spot, never around the room. Forty-five children moving between desks costs four minutes and you do not get them back.

blocks.name: Pass the picture, say the word
blocks.prep: One page or object per row - a picture from a textbook is enough
blocks.language: Any noun set the class is learning
steps: Give the first pupil in each row a picture or an object.
On your signal it passes along the row. Every pupil who receives it says the word aloud before passing it on.
The row that reaches the end first, with everybody having said the word, wins.
Send a different picture down each row and run it again, so each row practises a new word.
blocks.variation: Harder: the pupil must say a short sentence - *this is a ball* - not just the noun.
blocks.bigClass: Passing along the row is the only way every one of forty-five pupils speaks in six minutes. Walk beside a different row each round, because the middle of a row is where a child stays silent.

items.q: They shout. Is that a problem?
a: Not in itself - a Grade 1 class saying a word loudly together is doing exactly what it should. What matters is that the noise stops when you ask. Practise the stopping signal on the first day with nothing at stake, use the same one every time, and the volume stops being a discipline question.

items.q: Some pupils say nothing at all.
a: At this age a silent child is usually still listening, and pressing them to speak alone in front of forty-four others makes it worse rather than better. Whole-class repetition and group chanting let them join when ready, which is why most of the games below have the whole class speaking at once rather than one pupil at a time.

items.q: How long should a Grade 1 game last?
a: Four to six minutes. A six-year-old's attention for one activity is shorter than the length of most games as written, and two short rounds on different days teach more than one long round that ended badly.

pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 2, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 2 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: short sentences instead of single words - plurals, this and that, family, the body, and simple questions.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 2 class needs from a game
text: Grade 2 is where a pupil stops naming things and starts saying something about them. *Ball* becomes *this is a ball*, and then *these are two balls*. That step is the whole year, and it is harder than it looks, because a child who can name fifty objects may still not produce a single sentence unprompted.
So the games below all have a sentence in them, not a word. The rule of each one makes the sentence the only way to score, because a child who can win by pointing will point.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: One or many
blocks.grouping: Whole class, then two teams by half the room
blocks.language: Singular and plural: *this is a book / these are three books*
steps: Hold up one pen: the class says *this is a pen.* Hold up three: *these are three pens.*
Do six or seven objects with the whole class together, alternating one and many unpredictably.
Split the room in two. Hold up objects; the half that says the correct full sentence first scores. A half that says only the noun scores nothing, and say so before you start.
Finish with something awkward on purpose - two dusters, or a handful of chalk - and let them argue about it in English.
blocks.variation: Harder: use objects whose plural is irregular, and teach *these are three children* as a whole phrase rather than as a rule.
blocks.bigClass: Halves rather than rows, because the sentence has to be said together and forty-five pupils in two groups can chant a sentence in unison where six teams cannot.

blocks.name: This one or that one
blocks.language: *This* and *that*, near and far
steps: Stand next to a desk and say *this is a desk.* Point at the door across the room: *that is a door.*
Everybody stands. Point at something near you and the class says the sentence with *this*; point at something far and they use *that*.
Then let a pupil do the pointing while the class supplies the sentence.
End by pointing at something at the very edge of near and far, and let the class decide which word it takes.
blocks.variation: Add *these* and *those* once *this* and *that* are secure, but not in the same round.
blocks.bigClass: Standing matters here: the words mean near me and far from me, and a child sitting down has no sense of the distance.

blocks.name: The family chair
blocks.grouping: Whole class, one chair at the front
blocks.language: Family words, and *he is / she is my...*
steps: Put one chair at the front. A pupil sits in it and is not themselves any more: they are a family member the class must guess.
The class asks yes-or-no questions: *Are you a man? Are you old? Do you cook?*
The pupil answers only *yes* or *no*, which is why even a shy child can take the chair.
When the class guesses, everybody says the sentence together: *She is your grandmother.*
blocks.variation: Easier: write five family words on the board first so the guessing has a short list.
blocks.bigClass: Take questions by row - row one asks, then row two - or forty-five children shout at once. Two pupils in the chair per game is plenty.

blocks.name: Head, hands and freeze
blocks.language: Parts of the body, and *touch your...*
steps: Give instructions: *touch your head, touch your ears, touch your knees.* The class follows.
Speed up, then say *freeze* - everybody stops, hands where they are.
While frozen, ask individual pupils *what are you touching?* and they answer *my nose.* The freeze is what makes a one-pupil answer possible without the rest getting restless.
Unfreeze and continue, with a freeze every thirty seconds or so.
blocks.variation: Harder: give the instruction wrongly on purpose, touching your ear while saying *touch your nose*, and see who follows the words rather than the hands.
blocks.bigClass: The freeze is the whole reason this works with forty-five: you get individual answers without ever losing the other forty-four.

blocks.name: Who does it?
blocks.language: Simple present, third person: *he cooks, she teaches, he drives*
steps: Board four or five jobs the class knows: teacher, driver, cook, farmer, doctor.
Say what somebody does: *This person drives a bus.* The first row to say the full sentence *He is a driver* or *She is a driver* scores.
Then reverse it: you name the job and the row must say what the person does - *A cook cooks food.*
Note on the board any row that said *he drive* instead of *he drives*, without a name, and fix all of them together at the end.
blocks.variation: Harder: use jobs the class has not been taught and let them describe rather than name.
blocks.bigClass: Rows are ideal here because the missing -s is the point of the game, and a row correcting itself before answering is the lesson happening without you.

blocks.name: My bag has
blocks.prep: None - the pupils use their own bags
blocks.language: *There is / there are*, and school objects
steps: Show your own bag and say *in my bag there is a book and there are two pens.*
In pairs, each pupil tells their partner what is in their bag, using *there is* and *there are*.
Walk round and listen. Pick three pupils whose sentences were correct and let them say them to the class.
Then play it as a memory round: one pupil says their sentence, the next pupil repeats it and adds their own.
blocks.variation: Harder: the memory chain continues to six or seven pupils before resetting.
blocks.bigClass: Pair work first means all forty-five speak before anybody performs, so the three who speak to the class have already practised once.

blocks.name: Yes I do, no I don't
blocks.language: *Do you like...?* with the short answers
steps: Ask *do you like milk rice?* Pupils who do stand and say *yes, I do*; the rest stay seated and say *no, I don't.*
Go through eight or nine foods, so that the class is up and down and everybody says both answers several times.
Then let a pupil ask the question. They will need the question form, so board *Do you like ___?* before you hand it over.
Count the standing pupils for two or three items and write the numbers on the board: the class has made a small survey without being told so.
blocks.variation: Harder: follow a *yes* with *why?* for two or three pupils only.
blocks.bigClass: Standing to answer means you can see forty-five answers at once, and a child who is unsure can watch their neighbour - which at this level is learning, not cheating.

blocks.name: Colour it as I say
blocks.prep: None - pupils draw four shapes in their own books
blocks.language: Colours, shapes and prepositions: *in, on, under, next to*
steps: Everybody draws a big square, a circle, a triangle and a line in their book. Two minutes, no more.
Now give instructions: *colour the circle red. Put a small cross in the square. Draw a flower next to the triangle.*
Give six or seven instructions, saying each one twice and no more.

At the end, hold up your own version and let them compare. The pupils who followed every instruction will have the same picture, and the differences show you exactly which preposition was not understood.
blocks.variation: Harder: two instructions at once - *colour the circle red and the square blue.*
blocks.bigClass: This is the quietest game on this page and the easiest to run with forty-five, because every pupil works alone and the comparison at the end does the marking for you.

items.q: Should Grade 2 pupils write during a game?
a: Very little, and only by copying. The programme at this level is oral, and a game that stops for writing stops being a game. If you want the language written down, put the best three sentences on the board at the end and let the class copy those - which takes two minutes and gives the pupils who need to see a word the chance to see it.

items.q: They answer in Sinhala or Tamil.
a: Expect it, and do not punish it. Accept the answer, say it back in English, and have the class repeat your version. A child who has understood and answered in their own language has done the harder half of the work; the English is the part you can supply.

items.q: The same five pupils always win.
a: Change what winning means. Score by row rather than by individual, or give a point for any correct sentence rather than the first correct sentence. Most of these games can be scored either way, and scoring by row means the confident pupil's job becomes helping their row rather than beating it.

pages.title: Grade 3 English Classroom Games
pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 3, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.
pages.keywords: grade 3 english games, english classroom games grade 3, esl games grade 3, english language games for large classes, no preparation english games

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 3 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: can and can't, where things are, days and weather, likes and dislikes, and the first written sentences.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 3 class needs from a game
text: Grade 3 is the year reading and writing English start to carry weight, so a game may now ask for a written word - but a short one, and never as the main event. A game that becomes a writing exercise has stopped being a game and the class will notice before you do.

The language of this year is about what a pupil can do, where things are, and what they like, and all three are easy to turn into a rule that forces the target language out. That is why these games work: the sentence is the only way to score.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: Can you, can't you
blocks.language: *Can* and *can't* for ability: *I can swim. I can't drive.*
steps: Board six actions: swim, ride a bicycle, cook rice, drive, sing, climb a tree.
Each row decides, quietly, one thing that every single pupil in the row can do. Two minutes.
A row announces it: *We can all sing.* Any row that can truthfully say the same scores a point too - so the game rewards a row for guessing what the others can do, not just themselves.
Then reverse it: one thing nobody in the row can do, using *can't*.
blocks.variation: Harder: the row must find something they can all do that no other row can, which takes real negotiation in English.
blocks.bigClass: The row is the team and nobody moves. The quiet negotiation inside each row is where most of the speaking happens, so let it run and walk between the rows listening rather than watching the front.

blocks.name: Where is the duster?
blocks.grouping: Whole class, one pupil out at a time
blocks.language: Prepositions of place: *in, on, under, behind, next to, between*
steps: One pupil closes their eyes. Hide a duster somewhere in the room while the class watches.
The pupil opens their eyes and asks *is it under the table?* The class answers *no, it isn't* or *yes, it is.*
Three questions only, then a new pupil. The short limit keeps it moving and means eight pupils get a turn.
When it is found, the whole class says where it was in a full sentence: *It was behind the door.*
blocks.variation: Harder: the class may only answer *warm* or *cold*, so the guesser must produce far more sentences.
blocks.bigClass: The forty-four who are not guessing are the ones answering, in unison, so nobody is idle. Insist on the full short answer rather than a nod.

blocks.name: Monday to Sunday scramble
blocks.grouping: Seven pupils at the front, the rest directing
blocks.prep: Seven slips of paper with the days written on them
blocks.language: Days of the week, and *before, after, first, last*
steps: Give seven pupils one day each. They stand at the front in the wrong order, holding the papers so the class can read them.
The class directs them into the right order, speaking only in English: *Wednesday, go after Tuesday.*
Once they are right, the whole class reads the days aloud in order, then backwards.
Swap the seven pupils and run it again with a different starting muddle.
blocks.variation: Harder: use the months, with twelve pupils and the class directing.
blocks.bigClass: Only seven pupils are at the front, so take the instructions row by row - row one gives the first instruction, row two the next - and every row speaks.

blocks.name: I like, I don't like
blocks.language: *Like* and *don't like* with food, and *so do I*
steps: Board eight foods, mixing the obvious with the arguable: rice, bread, fish, brinjal, mango, coconut sambol, tea, bitter gourd.
In pairs, each pupil says which they like and which they do not, in full sentences. The partner replies *so do I* or *I don't.*
Walk round and find two pairs who disagreed about something. Let each pair say their disagreement to the class.
Finish with a class count on the most argued-about food and write the two numbers on the board.
blocks.variation: Harder: add *because* - *I don't like bitter gourd because it is bitter* - which is the first real reason-giving of the year.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs sitting side by side, no movement. The two pairs who report have already said their sentences once, which is why they can say them to forty-five people.

blocks.name: The weather window
blocks.language: Weather words, and *it is raining / it is sunny*
steps: Look out of the window together and say what the weather is, in a full sentence.
Then call out places and let the class guess the weather: *Nuwara Eliya in December. Hambantota in July.*
Now mime: you act a weather without speaking - shivering, fanning yourself, opening an umbrella - and the class says the sentence.
Let three pupils come and mime a weather for the class.
blocks.variation: Harder: ask what they wear in that weather, which brings in clothes vocabulary without a new lesson.
blocks.bigClass: Miming from the front is visible to forty-five in a way that a picture held up is not. Choose the three pupils from the back rows, who are usually chosen last.

blocks.name: Draw what I say
blocks.language: Prepositions, colours and numbers together
steps: Everybody has a blank half-page. You describe a simple picture slowly: *There is a house. There is a tree next to the house. There are three birds above the tree.*
Say each sentence twice only. Six or seven sentences is plenty.
Then draw your own version on the board and let them compare in pairs, in English: *I have two birds. You have three.*
The differences tell you exactly which preposition the class has not got, which is worth more than the drawings.
blocks.variation: Harder: a pupil describes and the class draws, which is much harder for the describer than for the class.
blocks.bigClass: The quietest game here and the best for a large class, because every pupil is working and the comparison at the end is done in pairs rather than by you.

blocks.name: The time race
blocks.language: Telling the time on the hour and half hour, and *what time do you...?*
steps: Draw a large blank clock face on the board.
Call a time - *half past four* - and the first pupil from each row comes and draws the hands. Fastest correct row scores.
After four or five rounds, change it: you draw the hands and the rows say the time in a full sentence.
End with real times: *What time do you get up? What time does school start?* answered around the rows.
blocks.variation: Harder: quarter past and quarter to, which is where most Grade 3 classes come unstuck.
blocks.bigClass: One pupil per row at the board means five or six at once, which is manageable; twenty is not. Send the next pupil in each row every round so it works down the rows automatically.

blocks.name: Three things about me
blocks.language: Simple present sentences about oneself, and listening for detail
steps: Say three sentences about yourself, one of which is false: *I have two brothers. I can ride a bicycle. I don't like tea.*
The class votes on which is false, then you tell them.
Give every pupil two minutes to think of their own three, with one false. Board the sentence starters they need: *I have..., I can..., I don't like...*
Take six or seven pupils, spread across the rows. Each says their three and the class votes.
blocks.variation: Harder: the class may ask one question before voting, which forces a question form out of them.
blocks.bigClass: Everybody prepares, only seven perform, and the other thirty-eight are listening and voting rather than waiting. Note down who spoke and start with those pupils' rows next time.

items.q: Is it worth playing a game when the syllabus is behind?
a: A game is only worth the period if it produces more language per pupil than the alternative, and with forty-five pupils it very often does. Twenty minutes of a game in which every pupil says eight sentences beats twenty minutes of a lesson in which nine pupils say one each. Judge it by that, not by how it feels.

items.q: How do I stop it becoming a shouting match?
a: Score by row and write the score on the board where everybody can see it. Most of the noise in a class game is not excitement, it is dispute about who was first and what the score is. Remove the dispute and the volume halves.

items.q: Can I use these for a mixed-ability class?
a: Every game below has a variation line, and most of them can be made easier by putting the words on the board before you start and harder by taking them off. In a mixed class, board the words, and let the pupils who do not need them not look.

pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 4, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 4 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: the past simple, comparing two things, describing a person or a room, and telling somebody what you did.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 4 class needs from a game
text: Two things arrive in Grade 4 and both change what a game can do. The past simple means a pupil can say what happened, so a game can have a story in it for the first time. Comparatives mean a pupil needs a second thing to hold up against the first, so most of these games work in twos.

The past simple is also where the irregular verbs start causing trouble, and a game is the kindest place for that trouble to happen. A pupil who says *I goed* in a game hears the correct form from their own row within two seconds, which is faster and less painful than hearing it from you.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: The yesterday chain
blocks.language: Past simple: *I got up, I ate, I went, I came*
steps: Board six past-tense verbs the class will need, including two irregular ones.
The first pupil in a row says one thing they did yesterday: *Yesterday I ate rice.*
The next pupil repeats it and adds their own: *He ate rice. Yesterday I played cricket.* The repetition is the listening practice and it is the harder half.
Go five or six pupils down the row, then start a fresh chain in the next row so no chain becomes impossible.
blocks.variation: Harder: the chain must be in time order through the day - got up, ate, came to school - so the pupils must place their sentence rather than just add it.
blocks.bigClass: Five short chains in five rows at once is not possible, so run one row at a time while the others listen for mistakes: give the listening rows the job of catching a wrong verb, and they will.

blocks.name: Taller than me
blocks.language: Comparatives: *taller, shorter, older, younger, bigger*
steps: Stand two pupils of clearly different heights at the front. The class says both sentences: *Nimal is taller than Sunil. Sunil is shorter than Nimal.*
Now everybody stands and finds a neighbour. Each pair says the two sentences about themselves.
Then change the adjective: older and younger, which they must ask about rather than see. Board *How old are you?* first.
Finish with the whole class ordering four pupils at the front from shortest to tallest, directing them in English.
blocks.variation: Harder: the superlative - *the tallest in this row* - once the comparative is secure.
blocks.bigClass: Neighbours, never partners across the room. Four pupils at the front is enough for the ordering; eight turns it into a scrum.

blocks.name: Guess my person
blocks.language: Describing people: hair, height, clothes, and *he has / she is wearing*
steps: Think of a pupil in the room and describe them without naming them: *She has long hair. She is wearing a blue ribbon. She is sitting near the window.*
The class guesses. Insist the guess is a name only after three of your sentences, so they must listen to all three.
Then a pupil takes over. Board the three sentence starters they will need before handing over.
Rule: nothing unkind, and nothing about size. Say this once at the start and it will not be a problem.
blocks.variation: Harder: describe a teacher the whole school knows, or a person in a picture in the textbook.
blocks.bigClass: Ideal for forty-five, because the class is the guesser and every pupil is looking around the room for the person. Take the guesses by row to stop the shouting.

blocks.name: My day in six sentences
blocks.language: Daily routine in the past simple, with time words
steps: Board six time phrases: *at six o'clock, after that, then, at school, in the evening, before I slept.*
Every pupil writes six sentences about yesterday, one for each time phrase. Six minutes, no more, and short sentences are correct.
In pairs, they read their six to each other and find one thing they both did.
Take four pupils and let each read one sentence only - their best one. Four sentences read aloud is enough to show the class what good looks like.
blocks.variation: Easier: three sentences instead of six. Harder: the last sentence must say how the day was and why.
blocks.bigClass: This is the writing game, and in a large class the pair reading is what makes it speaking too. Never take more than four readers or the last two lose the class.

blocks.name: The furniture map
blocks.language: Rooms and furniture with prepositions: *the table is in the middle, the bed is against the wall*
steps: Each pupil draws the plan of a room - their own, or an imaginary one - with four or five pieces of furniture. Three minutes.
They do not show it to their partner. Instead they describe it while the partner draws.
Compare the two drawings. The differences are all preposition problems, and the pair will find them without you.
Swap roles with a new room.
blocks.variation: Harder: the describer may not use the furniture's name, only what it is for - *the thing you sleep on*.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs at their desks, nobody moving, forty-five pupils all speaking at once. Walk between the rows and note two preposition errors to fix on the board at the end.

blocks.name: The shopping list
blocks.language: Food and quantities: *a kilo of, a bottle of, two hundred grams of*
steps: Board the quantity phrases: *a kilo of, half a kilo of, a bottle of, a packet of, a bunch of.*
Give each row a task: *You have a thousand rupees and you are cooking rice and curry for six people. Make the list.*
Five minutes, one sheet passed along the row so every pupil writes one item.
Each row reads its list. The class judges which list would actually make the meal, which requires them to listen to every item.
blocks.variation: Harder: a fixed budget that does not quite stretch, so the row must argue about what to leave out - in English.
blocks.bigClass: One sheet per row, passed along, is what stops the strongest pupil writing all ten items. Say that rule out loud or it will happen anyway.

blocks.name: Which one is different
blocks.language: Any vocabulary set, plus *because* for the reason
steps: Say four words, three of which share something: *mango, banana, rice, papaya.*
A pupil says which is different and why, in a full sentence with *because*: *Rice is different because it is not a fruit.*
The trick is that more than one answer is usually defensible. Accept any answer the pupil can justify, and say so before you start.
After five rounds, let pupils set the puzzles. Theirs will be harder than yours.
blocks.variation: Harder: four words with two possible odd ones out, and the class must find both reasons.
blocks.bigClass: Take answers by row in turn. The *because* is the whole point of the game - without it this is a guessing game and teaches nothing.

blocks.name: The long sentence
blocks.language: Extending a sentence with adjectives, place and time
steps: Give each row a bare sentence: *The boy ran.*
Each pupil in the row adds one word or one phrase and says the whole sentence from the beginning: *The small boy ran. The small boy ran quickly. The small boy ran quickly to school.*
A row scores one point for each addition that still makes a correct sentence. A row that breaks the grammar stops there.
Board the longest correct sentence from each row at the end and let the class choose the best one - which is not the same as the longest.
blocks.variation: Harder: no adjectives allowed, only phrases of time and place.
blocks.bigClass: The repetition from the beginning is what makes this work with forty-five: every pupil says the whole sentence, so the row hears it five or six times and remembers the pattern.

items.q: They keep saying *goed* and *eated*.
a: They will, for two years. Board the six or seven irregular verbs the game needs before you start and leave them up. A pupil who can see *went* will use *went*, and seeing it forty times in a game is how it eventually becomes automatic. Taking the list down too early is the commonest mistake here.

items.q: Is a game useful for the term test?
a: Only if the language in the game is the language on the paper. That is why each game below names what it practises. If the term test has a past-tense paragraph on it, the games with a story in them are test preparation, whatever they look like from the corridor.

items.q: My class is forty-eight. Is that too many?
a: No. Every game on this page is written for a class of that size and none of them needs pupils to move from their seats. The two things that actually break down in a large class are movement and individual turns, so these avoid both.

pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 5, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 5 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: reading closely, putting sentences in order, giving reasons, and writing three or four connected sentences.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 5 class needs from a game
text: Grade 5 is the scholarship year, English is not in that paper, and the English period is the one most likely to be taken for revision. That is the real condition these games are written for, so every one of them is short, and every one produces something a scholarship paper also asks for: reading closely, putting things in order, and giving a reason.

None of that is a compromise. A pupil who can order four sentences and say why is doing the same thinking the mathematics paper wants, in English. It is worth saying so out loud to a colleague who asks.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: The paragraph jumble
blocks.prep: Four or five sentences of a story written on the board out of order
blocks.language: Sequencing, and the words that signal order: *first, then, after that, finally*
steps: Board five sentences of a short story in the wrong order, numbered 1 to 5 as they stand.
In pairs, pupils write the correct order as a line of numbers. Three minutes.
Take the answer from one pair, then ask a different pair whether they agree and why. The *why* is the lesson: *Sentence 4 must be first because it says he woke up.*
Read the story aloud in the right order with the whole class.
blocks.variation: Harder: one of the five sentences does not belong in the story at all, and they must find it.
blocks.bigClass: Everything is on the board, so nothing is copied or handed out. Pairs sitting together, no movement, and the numbers make marking instant from the front.

blocks.name: What happened next
blocks.language: Past simple narrative, and *because* and *so*
steps: Give the class one opening sentence: *When Amali opened her bag, her lunch was not there.*
Each row builds the story, one sentence per pupil, spoken aloud, down the row.
The rule is that each sentence must follow from the one before. A pupil whose sentence does not follow is asked *why did that happen?* and must connect it with *because* or *so*.
At the end, ask the class which row's story was best and why. Insist on a reason.
blocks.variation: Harder: the story must end with a sentence you give them at the start, so the row has to steer towards it.
blocks.bigClass: One row at a time with the others judging. Give the listening rows a job - decide which sentence was the cleverest - and they will listen to all of it.

blocks.name: Fact or opinion
blocks.language: Distinguishing a fact from an opinion, and *I think*
steps: Explain the difference with two examples: *Kandy is in the Central Province* and *Kandy is the most beautiful city.*
Read out ten sentences. Pupils stand for a fact and stay seated for an opinion.
After each one, ask one pupil why. The reason matters more than the answer.
Include two that genuinely could be argued, and let the class argue them.
blocks.variation: Harder: pupils write three sentences about their own village, two facts and one opinion, and the class identifies which is which.
blocks.bigClass: Standing to answer shows you forty-five answers at once, and the pupils who look around before deciding are the ones to ask why.

blocks.name: Twenty questions about a picture
blocks.grouping: Whole class, one pupil at the front
blocks.prep: None - any picture in the textbook
blocks.language: Question forms, and yes-or-no short answers
steps: A pupil chooses one thing in a picture everybody can see and does not say what it is.
The class asks yes-or-no questions: *Is it an animal? Is it on the left? Is it bigger than a chair?*
Count the questions on the board. Fewer than ten is good guessing; more than fifteen means the questions were poor, and it is worth saying which ones wasted a turn.
Two or three rounds, with a different pupil each time.
blocks.variation: Harder: the class may not ask about position at all, only about what the thing is and does.
blocks.bigClass: Take questions strictly by row in order. The counting on the board is what makes the class think before asking, which is the actual skill.

blocks.name: The comparison ladder
blocks.language: Comparatives and superlatives together
steps: Board four things of clearly different size: an ant, a cat, an elephant, a bus.
Each row writes as many true comparison sentences as it can in three minutes, one sheet passed along.
Read them out. A point for each correct sentence, two for a sentence using the superlative correctly.
Board the two best sentences and let the class improve them further.
blocks.variation: Harder: four things that are not obviously ordered - a book, a telephone, a bicycle, a shoe - so the comparison has to name what is being compared.
blocks.bigClass: One sheet per row passed along means every pupil writes one sentence, which is forty-five sentences in three minutes. No other arrangement gets close.

blocks.name: Spot the wrong sentence
blocks.prep: Four sentences on the board, one with a mistake
blocks.language: Whatever the class is getting wrong: subject-verb agreement, plurals, tense
steps: Board four sentences. One has a single error, taken from the class's own written work - never with a name attached.
Pairs find it and write the correction. Two minutes.
Take the answer, then ask whether anybody thought a different sentence was wrong. Wrong answers here are useful and should be discussed, not dismissed.
Do three rounds. The errors should be the ones you keep marking, so they meet them before the next test.
blocks.variation: Harder: two of the four have errors, and nobody is told how many.
blocks.bigClass: Everything on the board, nothing distributed. Using the class's own errors anonymously is what makes this worth the five minutes: they are the mistakes actually being made in that room.

blocks.name: One sentence only
blocks.prep: A short paragraph the class has already read
blocks.language: Summarising, and choosing what matters
steps: Take a paragraph from the reader that the class knows. Everybody writes what it is about in exactly one sentence.
Four or five pupils read theirs out. Do not judge them yet.
Ask the class which one sentence would help somebody who had not read the paragraph. That is the test of a summary, and it is not the longest one.
Board the best and let the class shorten it by three words without losing the meaning.
blocks.variation: Harder: a limit of eight words, which forces real decisions.
blocks.bigClass: Everybody writes, five read, and the shortening at the end is done by the whole class together - so the thirty-nine who did not read are still doing the work.

blocks.name: The instruction test
blocks.language: Reading and following written instructions precisely
steps: Board six numbered instructions. Number one says: *Read all six instructions before you do anything.* Number six says: *Do only number two.*
Give them three minutes and say nothing while they work.
Most of the class will do all six. Let that happen without warning them, then read number one aloud again.
Talk about it for two minutes: on an examination paper, the instruction at the top is the one that decides the marks.
blocks.variation: Use it once a term, no more. It works exactly once with any class, and the class will tell the next one.
blocks.bigClass: Better with forty-five than with ten, because the two or three pupils who read to the end first will sit quietly and the rest will notice them - which teaches the point faster than you can.

items.q: My English period keeps being taken for scholarship revision.
a: It will be, and arguing about the timetable rarely works. What does work is making the English period visibly produce reasoning and reading, which is why every game here can be finished in under ten minutes and leaves something on the page. Ten minutes of English inside a revision period is worth more than a fight you lose.

items.q: Half my class will not sit the scholarship and knows it.
a: Those are frequently the pupils for whom the English period matters most, because it is the subject where they are not already behind. Score by row rather than individually so the pupils who have given up on marks can still contribute, and choose the readers and speakers from among them.

items.q: Should I correct their English or their reasoning?
a: The reasoning first, and out loud. If a pupil gives a sound reason in poor English, say the reason was good and then supply the English. A pupil corrected only on grammar stops offering reasons, and the reasons are the part that is harder to teach.

pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 6, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 6 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: introductions, the present simple and continuous, asking questions, and describing what is in front of you.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 6 class needs from a game
text: Grade 6 classes arrive from several primary schools at once, and the spread of English in the room on the first day is wider than it will ever be again. A game that only the strongest quarter can play will teach you which quarter that is and nothing else.

So these are chosen for a mixed room. In most of them the rule sets the floor - a pupil with very little English can still take a full turn - and the variation line says how to raise the ceiling for the pupils who are already fluent, in the same game, at the same time.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: Introduce your partner
blocks.language: *This is..., he lives..., she likes...* - third person present simple
steps: Board four questions: *What is your name? Where do you live? What do you like? What school were you in?*
In pairs, each pupil asks their partner all four and remembers the answers. No writing - it makes them listen.
Then each pupil introduces their partner to the class in three sentences: *This is Nirasha. She lives in Weliweriya. She likes netball.*
Take as many pairs as the period allows, and finish the rest next lesson rather than rushing them.
blocks.variation: Harder: the introducer may not look at their partner while speaking, and the partner may not correct them until the end.
blocks.bigClass: Twelve or fourteen introductions is a full period and that is fine; do a few rows each lesson for a week. The third person -s is the teaching point, and by the fortieth introduction the class hears it correctly.

blocks.name: What is happening now
blocks.language: Present continuous: *he is writing, they are talking*
steps: Do something small and obvious - open a book, look out of the window, write on the board - and ask *what am I doing?* The class answers in a full sentence.
Then describe what somebody in the room is doing without naming them, and the class guesses who.
Now the reverse: name a pupil, and the class says what that pupil is doing at that moment.
Finish with five seconds of silence and ask *what is happening in this room now?* - which produces sentences like *nobody is talking*, and that is a harder sentence than it looks.
blocks.variation: Harder: add *while* - *Sunil is writing while Kamala is reading.*
blocks.bigClass: Everything is visible from anywhere in the room, so a class of fifty works as well as a class of twenty. Describe pupils from the back rows, who are rarely the subject of anything.

blocks.name: The classroom survey
blocks.language: Questions in the present simple, and *how many*
steps: Give each row one question to ask: *Do you walk to school? Do you have a brother? Do you like cricket? Do you watch the news?*
Each row asks its question of everybody in the row and counts the yes answers. Three minutes.
Each row reports: *In our row, seven pupils walk to school and two do not.*
Board the totals for the whole class and ask two comparison questions about them.
blocks.variation: Harder: each row invents its own question, which must be answerable with yes or no - itself a useful lesson.
blocks.bigClass: Rows do their own counting simultaneously, so the class of forty-five is surveyed in three minutes. Without rows this activity takes a full period and produces less.

blocks.name: Spelling relay
blocks.language: Spelling aloud, and the alphabet
steps: Call a word the class has learned. The first pupil in each row says the first letter, the second pupil the second letter, and so on along the row.
If a pupil gives a wrong letter, the row starts that word again from the beginning - which makes the whole row listen rather than count ahead to their own turn.
The first row to spell the word correctly to the end scores.
Five or six words, choosing ones the class actually misspells in their books.
blocks.variation: Harder: longer words, or the row must say the word at the end before the point counts.
blocks.bigClass: Every pupil in every row speaks in every round, which is forty-five letters said aloud per word. Restarting on an error is the rule that does the teaching, so do not soften it.

blocks.name: The timetable gap
blocks.language: School subjects, days and times, and *what do you have on...?*
steps: Each pupil draws a blank timetable grid for three days and fills in only half the boxes, inventing them freely.
Without showing each other, partners ask and answer to complete a copy of the other's timetable: *What do you have on Monday at ten?*
When both are done they compare grids and count the mistakes.
The mistakes are almost always mishearings of the time, which is worth two minutes at the end.
blocks.variation: Easier: use the class's real timetable and blank out different boxes for each partner.
blocks.bigClass: An information gap is the most reliable way to make forty-five pupils speak at once with a purpose, and it needs nothing but their exercise books.

blocks.name: True for me, true for you
blocks.language: Present simple statements, and *so do I / I don't*
steps: Say a sentence about yourself: *I drink tea in the morning.* Pupils for whom it is also true stand and say *so do I.*
Those for whom it is not stay seated and say *I don't.*
After five of yours, pupils offer their own sentences. Board the starters they will need.
The best moments are the sentences where almost the whole class stands, or almost nobody does, and it is worth pointing those out.
blocks.variation: Harder: negative sentences, which need *neither do I* - a genuinely difficult form, worth a whole round on its own.
blocks.bigClass: You can read forty-five answers in one glance. Pupils who look around before standing are the ones who have not understood, and that is useful information you cannot get from a worksheet.

blocks.name: Find somebody who
blocks.language: Question forms, and reporting an answer
steps: Board six prompts: *has a bicycle, can cook, was born in this town, likes mathematics, has been to Colombo, watches cricket.*
Pupils ask the four people nearest them - in front, behind and either side - to find one person for each prompt. Nobody stands up.
The prompt must be turned into a real question: *Can you cook?*, not *can cook?*. Say this before starting or it will not happen.
Report back: *Dilani can cook. Ravi has a bicycle.* Each pupil reports one only, going along the rows.
blocks.variation: Harder: a pupil may not use the same person twice, which forces them to ask more people.
blocks.bigClass: The usual version of this game has the class walking around, which costs six minutes and a great deal of noise in a room of forty-five. Asking the four nearest people produces the same language and none of the chaos.

blocks.name: The description box
blocks.language: Describing a place: *there is, there are*, and prepositions
steps: Each pupil writes five sentences describing a place in the school - the canteen, the library, the field - without naming it.
In pairs they read their description and the partner guesses the place.
Take four descriptions for the whole class to guess.
Then improve one together on the board: ask the class which sentence gave it away, and which sentence was useless.
blocks.variation: Harder: the description may not contain any noun that is only found in that place, so *books* is banned for the library.
blocks.bigClass: Everybody writes and everybody guesses in pairs; only four go public. The improvement at the end is the real lesson and it involves the whole class at once.

items.q: The class is enormous and I do not know their names yet.
a: Use the rows as the unit for the first month and do not try to learn forty-five names before you start playing. Several games below have pupils introduce themselves or each other, which is the fastest way to learn the names while teaching something.

items.q: A third of my class can barely read English.
a: Then avoid the games that need reading from the board for the first weeks, and use the oral ones. Every game here says what it needs. A pupil who cannot yet read can still say a sentence, and being able to take a full turn in front of the class is the thing that keeps them coming back to English.

items.q: Do these work for the new Grade 6 syllabus?
a: The language they practise - introductions, the present tenses, questions, describing - is what any Grade 6 English course covers in its first terms, so they fit the scheme rather than depending on it. Check the competency level you are working on and pick the game that produces that language.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 7 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: telling what happened - the past simple and continuous, adverbs, giving instructions, and talking about the future.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 7 class needs from a game
text: Grade 7 is where a pupil stops listing and starts narrating. *I went to the shop* becomes *I was going to the shop when it started to rain*, and that second sentence is a real achievement: it has a background, an interruption, and a sense of time.

The games below are built around that. Several of them are stories built in turns, because a story built by a row teaches the shape of a narrative faster than any explanation of it - the pupil whose sentence does not fit is told so immediately, by the four people sitting behind them.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: The story in five verbs
blocks.language: Past simple, including irregular verbs
steps: Board five verbs in the base form: *go, see, run, fall, find.*
Each row writes a short story using all five in the past tense, in any order. Five minutes, one sheet passed along so each pupil writes one sentence.
Rows read their stories out. A point for each verb used correctly in the past, and a point if the story actually makes sense.
Board the irregular forms that went wrong - *runned*, *falled* - without naming the row, and fix them together.
blocks.variation: Harder: the verbs must be used in the order given, which forces the story to be planned rather than improvised.
blocks.bigClass: One sheet per row is the whole mechanism. Without it two pupils write everything and the other seven watch, which is the commonest way a good game fails in a big class.

blocks.name: How did he do it?
blocks.language: Adverbs of manner: *slowly, angrily, carefully, quietly, happily*
steps: Board eight adverbs. A pupil comes out and you whisper an adverb to them.
Give them an ordinary action - open the door, write your name, walk to the window - and they do it in the manner of the adverb.
The class guesses in a full sentence: *He opened the door angrily.*
Three or four pupils, then let the class set the actions as well as guess the adverbs.
blocks.variation: Harder: the adverb is not on the board, so the class must supply the word as well as the sentence.
blocks.bigClass: One actor, forty-four guessers, and the full sentence is what makes the forty-four work. Choose actors from different rows or the same four pupils will volunteer every time.

blocks.name: The witness
blocks.language: Past continuous for background, past simple for the event, and question forms
steps: Tell the class that something happened in the school at eleven o'clock yesterday - a window was broken, say - and that everybody is a witness.
Each pupil writes two sentences: what they were doing at eleven, and one thing they saw. *I was eating my lunch. I saw a boy running.*
In pairs, they question each other: *What were you doing? Who did you see? What was he wearing?*
Take four witnesses for the whole class to question, and let the class decide whose account was most useful and why.
blocks.variation: Harder: two of the witnesses are told privately to contradict each other, and the class must find the contradiction.
blocks.bigClass: Everybody writes, everybody questions a partner, four are questioned publicly. The contradiction variation is worth the extra minute because it makes forty-five pupils listen to every answer.

blocks.name: The recipe muddle
blocks.prep: Six instructions on the board, out of order
blocks.language: Imperatives and sequence words: *first, next, then, after that, finally*
steps: Board six steps of something the class knows how to do - making tea, making a paper boat - in the wrong order.
Pairs write the correct order and add a sequence word to each step.
Take the order from one pair, and ask another whether any step could reasonably come somewhere else. Usually one could, and that argument is the best part.
Then each pair writes three steps of a different process for another pair to order.
blocks.variation: Harder: one step is missing altogether and the pairs must work out what it is.
blocks.bigClass: Everything on the board, nothing handed out, pairs side by side. The pair-to-pair exchange at the end needs no movement if they simply swap books with the pair behind.

blocks.name: Catch the wrong verb
blocks.language: Past simple forms, especially irregular ones
steps: Tell a short story aloud, deliberately putting four wrong verb forms in it: *Yesterday I goed to the market and buyed three mangoes.*
The class claps or raises a hand the moment they hear a wrong form, and the pupil who catches it says the correct one.
Keep the story moving; do not stop for a long correction.
At the end, ask the class how many mistakes there were, and see whether they agree. They rarely do, which is the point.
blocks.variation: Harder: put in one mistake that is not a verb at all, and see whether anybody notices.
blocks.bigClass: The whole class listens to one voice, so size makes no difference. Deliberately mispronounce nothing - only the grammar is wrong, or you teach a pronunciation error by accident.

blocks.name: Better, worse, best
blocks.language: Comparatives and superlatives, including irregular ones
steps: Name two things the class has opinions about - cricket and football, town and village, morning school and afternoon school.
Each row writes three sentences comparing them and one superlative sentence. Four minutes.
Rows read out. A point for each correct comparison, two for a superlative used correctly.
Then take a vote on the comparison the class found most convincing, and ask why.
blocks.variation: Harder: ban *good* and *bad*, which forces adjectives the class has to reach for.
blocks.bigClass: Rows write simultaneously so the whole class is producing language for four solid minutes. Reading out takes two more, which is the right balance for a forty-minute period.

blocks.name: What will happen
blocks.language: *Will* for prediction, and *I think... will...*
steps: Give the class five things to predict: the weather tomorrow, who will win the next big match, what the class will be doing at this time next year.
In pairs they make one prediction each, in a full sentence with *I think*.
Collect a few, and write two of them in the corner of the board with the date.
Come back to those two predictions when the day arrives. A class that has seen its own prediction proved right remembers the form.
blocks.variation: Harder: add *because* to each prediction, which turns a guess into an argument.
blocks.bigClass: The board corner is the trick. It costs nothing, and returning to it weeks later is the strongest piece of teaching in this game.

blocks.name: The adjective ladder
blocks.language: Adjectives of degree: *warm, hot, boiling* - and precision of word choice
steps: Board a weak adjective: *big.*
Each row builds a ladder of adjectives from weakest to strongest, one word per pupil, spoken down the row: *big, large, huge, enormous.*
A row may challenge another row's order, and must say why. The argument is the lesson.
Do three ladders - *big*, *cold*, *nice* - and keep the best ladder from each on the board.
blocks.variation: Harder: start from a strong adjective and go downwards, which is much more difficult.
blocks.bigClass: Rows build simultaneously and then compare, so the whole class is thinking rather than waiting. The challenge rule is what makes them listen to the other rows.

items.q: When should I use the past continuous rather than the past simple?
a: The distinction the class needs is that the continuous is the background and the simple is the event: *I was walking* is the scene, *I saw* is what happened. Do not teach it as a rule about duration - pupils apply that rule wrongly for years. The witness game below makes the distinction do real work, which teaches it better than a definition.

items.q: My class is noisy during games and the next teacher complains.
a: Two things fix nearly all of it: score by row rather than individually, and use a stopping signal you have practised when nothing was at stake. It is also worth telling the teacher next door what you are doing and why - a period of purposeful noise is easier to accept when it is not a mystery.

items.q: Can I use the same game twice?
a: Yes, and you should. A game the class already knows needs no explanation, so the second time you get eight minutes of language instead of five minutes of instructions and three of language. Change the content, not the game.

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 8 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: the present perfect, reporting what somebody said, superlatives, and writing a short notice or message.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 8 class needs from a game
text: Two difficult things arrive in Grade 8: the present perfect, and reporting what somebody else said. Both are usually taught as rules, practised in an exercise, and then never produced again, because neither rule tells a pupil when they would actually want the form.

The games below give each form a job. *Have you ever...?* is the natural way to ask about somebody's whole life, and reported speech is the natural way to pass on a message - so the games are built around finding things out and passing things on, which is when those forms are genuinely needed.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: Have you ever
blocks.grouping: Rows, asking the pupils nearest them
blocks.language: Present perfect for experience, and past simple for the detail
steps: Board six experiences: *been to Colombo, eaten a durian, ridden a horse, lost something important, won a prize, slept in a train.*
Pupils ask the four people nearest them *Have you ever...?* and find one person for each.
Here is the rule that makes the game teach something: when somebody says yes, the asker must follow up with *When?* or *What happened?* - and the answer to that must be in the past simple.
Report back around the rows: *Ishara has been to Colombo. She went last April.* Two sentences, two tenses, which is the whole lesson.
blocks.variation: Harder: pupils invent their own six experiences, which must be things somebody in the room might plausibly have done.
blocks.bigClass: Nobody leaves their seat; the four nearest people are enough. The two-sentence report is what stops this being a vocabulary game, so insist on both sentences every time.

blocks.name: The message relay
blocks.language: Reported speech: *he said that..., she asked whether...*
steps: Whisper a short message to the first pupil in each row: *I am going to the library after school.*
It passes down the row, but each pupil must report it rather than repeat it: the second pupil says *He said he was going to the library after school.*
The last pupil in the row writes what reached them on the board.
Compare the boarded versions with the original. The distortions are always interesting, and they are almost always the tense.
blocks.variation: Harder: use a question - *Are you coming tomorrow?* - which forces *he asked whether*, a much harder form.
blocks.bigClass: Rows are the relay, so five relays run at once and every pupil in the room produces a reported sentence. Start all rows together or the later ones overhear the earlier ones.

blocks.name: Since or for
blocks.language: *Since* with a point in time, *for* with a length of time
steps: Board two headings, *since* and *for*, and call out time expressions: *2019, three years, I was small, ten minutes, last April, a long time.*
The class calls out which heading each belongs under, and a pupil comes and writes it.
Then each pupil writes two true sentences about themselves, one with each word: *I have lived in this town since 2018. I have known Amali for six years.*
Pairs check each other's two sentences before any are read out.
blocks.variation: Harder: a sentence that uses both - *I have been in this school for two years, since Grade 6.*
blocks.bigClass: Sorting into two columns can be done by the whole class calling out, and the writing is individual and quiet. The pair check means forty-five sentences are corrected without you reading one of them.

blocks.name: The tallest, the oldest, the best
blocks.language: Superlatives, including *the best* and *the worst*
steps: Each row must produce five true superlative sentences about the room, the school or the class: *Nuwan is the tallest boy in our row.*
Four minutes, one sheet passed along.
Rows read out. Any other row may challenge a sentence as untrue, and the class settles it.
A point per correct sentence, and a point deducted for a sentence successfully challenged - which makes them careful rather than fast.
blocks.variation: Harder: ban *the best* and *the worst*, which are the two the class will otherwise use five times each.
blocks.bigClass: The challenge rule is what keeps the other four rows listening while one row reads. Without it, a reading round in a class of forty-five is dead time.

blocks.name: The notice board
blocks.language: Writing a notice: what, when, where, who to contact
steps: Give a situation: the English Day competition entries close on Friday, or a lost water bottle, or a change to the cricket practice.
Each pair writes a notice of no more than forty words. The limit is the lesson.
Swap with the pair behind and check for the four things a notice must contain: what, when, where, and who to ask.
Board the best one and cut three more words out of it together.
blocks.variation: Harder: thirty words, which forces them to drop every unnecessary phrase.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs swapping with the pair behind them needs no movement at all. The joint cutting at the end is done by the whole class and is the part they remember.

blocks.name: Just, already, yet
blocks.language: The three adverbs with the present perfect, and their positions
steps: Board the three words and one sentence: *I have finished my homework.*
Put each word into the sentence in turn, with the class, and talk about what changes. *Yet* will need a negative or a question, and the class will discover that rather than be told it.
Then call situations - *the bell rang two seconds ago*, *you have not done something you should have* - and the class produces the sentence with the right adverb.
Finish with five sentences the class writes alone, one for each situation you name.
blocks.variation: Harder: include *still*, which behaves differently and is worth contrasting.
blocks.bigClass: The discovery about *yet* is the moment worth waiting for. Do not tell them; give a situation that needs it and let somebody in the room work it out.

blocks.name: The comparison debate
blocks.language: Comparatives, superlatives, and *because* and *but*
steps: Give the two halves opposite sides of a plain question: *Is it better to live in a town or a village?*
Four minutes to prepare three points each. One sheet per half, passed along, so everybody contributes a point.
Each side gives its three points, alternating. No interrupting.
Then each side must say which of the other side's points was the strongest - which is the hardest part and the most valuable.
blocks.variation: Harder: halfway through, swap sides, so each half must argue what it has just been arguing against.
blocks.bigClass: Two halves, not six teams: a debate needs enough people on a side to produce three good points in four minutes. The strongest-point rule stops it becoming a shouting match.

blocks.name: He said what?
blocks.language: Reporting statements, questions and requests
steps: In each three, one pupil is A, one is B, one is the reporter.
A and B have a thirty-second conversation on a topic you give - what they did at the weekend, what they are doing after school.
The reporter then tells the class, or the group next to them, what was said: *She said she had gone to her grandmother's. He asked whether she had enjoyed it.*
Rotate the roles twice so everybody reports once.
blocks.variation: Harder: the reporter may not take notes, which is how reporting works in life and makes them listen properly.
blocks.bigClass: Threes within a row, no movement. Fifteen groups reporting to the group beside them takes two minutes, where fifteen groups reporting to the whole class would take fifteen.

items.q: My class uses the past simple where the present perfect belongs.
a: So does most of the country, and it is not a catastrophe. The place to insist is where the meaning actually changes: *I have been to Kandy* means some time in my life, *I went to Kandy* means on a particular occasion. The Have you ever game below makes that difference do work, which is the only way it sticks.

items.q: Reported speech takes a whole period to explain.
a: Do not explain it first. Play the message relay below and let the class discover that *I am coming* has to become *he said he was coming* when you pass it on. Then name what they have just done. The rule explained after the need has been felt takes five minutes rather than forty.

items.q: How do I get the weaker pupils to write anything at all?
a: Give them a length limit rather than a topic: fifty words, not an essay. The notice game below works because a notice is short enough that a weak writer will start it, and the shortness is the point rather than a concession.

pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 9, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.
