hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 9 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: conditionals, the passive, and the difference between formal and friendly English.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 9 class needs from a game
text: Grade 9 is the last year before the Ordinary Level work takes over, and it is the right year for the two things O/L quietly assumes a pupil already has: the conditionals, and a sense of when English should be formal and when it should not.

The second of those is almost never taught directly, and it costs marks every year. A pupil who writes *Hi sir, please send me the form* in a letter to a principal has not made a grammatical mistake - they have made a judgement error, and judgement is trained by comparison rather than by rules. Three of the games below are comparisons of exactly that kind.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: If this, then that
blocks.language: First conditional: *if + present, will + base*
steps: Give the first pupil in each row an opening: *If it rains tomorrow...*
They complete it, then turn their result into the next condition: *...we will not have practice. If we do not have practice...*
The chain continues down the row, each pupil taking the last result as their new condition.
A row that breaks the form starts a new chain from where it broke. Read the longest chain out at the end.
blocks.variation: Harder: the chain must return to the starting idea by the last pupil in the row, which requires the row to steer.
blocks.bigClass: Five chains run at once, one per row, so forty-five conditionals are produced in seven minutes. Walk between rows and listen for *will* after *if*, which is the error to catch.

blocks.name: What would you do
blocks.language: Second conditional: *if I had..., I would...*
steps: Give four situations: *If you found a wallet with ten thousand rupees in it. If you could speak to anybody in the world. If your friend copied your homework. If you were principal for a day.*
In pairs, each pupil answers two of them in a full second conditional sentence.
Take answers to the wallet one from several pupils and let the class discuss whether they agree. This is the situation that produces real argument.
Board two of the best sentences and check the form together: *had*, not *would have*, in the if-clause.
blocks.variation: Harder: add *unless* to one situation, which is the form pupils avoid entirely unless forced.
blocks.bigClass: Everybody answers in a pair first, so the pupils who speak to the class have already said the sentence once. The wallet question will carry a class of any size.

blocks.name: Who did it?
blocks.language: The passive, and when the doer does not matter
steps: Board four active sentences about the school: *Somebody broke the window. They painted the hall last year.*
Ask the class who did each one. For most of them nobody knows or nobody cares - and that is exactly when English uses the passive.
Rewrite them together: *The window was broken. The hall was painted last year.*
Then each row finds three things in the school that were done by somebody unknown, and writes them in the passive.
blocks.variation: Harder: one of the four should be a sentence where the doer does matter, so the class has to decide the passive is wrong for it.
blocks.bigClass: The discovery step - asking who did it and finding that nobody knows - is what makes the form meaningful, and it works better with forty-five voices than with five.

blocks.name: The process line
blocks.language: The passive in sequence: *the rice is washed, then it is boiled*
steps: Give each row a process everybody knows: making tea, printing a newspaper, building a wall, cooking rice.
The row writes the process in six steps, all in the passive, one step per pupil down the sheet.
Rows read out. The class guesses the process from the steps alone if the row reads them without naming it.
A point for each correct passive, and a point if the class guessed the process.
blocks.variation: Harder: the row may not name the main ingredient at any point.
blocks.bigClass: One sheet, six steps, passed along the row - so six pupils write and the rest check. Give the checking job explicitly to the pupils who are not writing or they will simply wait.

blocks.name: Formal or friendly
blocks.language: Register: the same meaning in two kinds of English
steps: Board one message in two versions: *Sir, I am unable to attend school tomorrow as I have to accompany my mother to the hospital* and *sir cant come tomorrow amma is going to hospital.*
Ask the class what is different. They will say the second is wrong; push them past that to what it is wrong *for*.
Then give four situations - a message to a friend, a note to a principal, a caption on a photograph, a letter asking for a certificate - and pairs write one line for each.
Read some out and let the class place each one: which situation was it written for?
blocks.variation: Harder: write one line that would be wrong in every one of the four situations, which requires understanding all four.
blocks.bigClass: The boarded pair of messages does the teaching. Do not mark the informal one as bad English - say plainly that it is correct for one purpose and wrong for another, or the class stops trusting you.

blocks.name: The complaint desk
blocks.language: Polite forms: *could you, would it be possible, I would be grateful if*
steps: One pupil in each pair has a problem - a book not returned, a bus that never comes, a light that does not work in the classroom.
They must complain to their partner using only polite forms. Board four of them first.
The partner must refuse politely, twice, before agreeing to anything. The double refusal is what forces the complainer to find a second and third way of asking.
Swap roles with a new problem.
blocks.variation: Harder: the complainer may not use the word *please* at all, which removes their one crutch.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs at their desks, everybody talking at once. The double-refusal rule is the whole design - without it each pair finishes in twenty seconds.

blocks.name: The missing cause
blocks.language: *Because, so, although, however*
steps: Board four results with no causes: *...so the match was cancelled. ...although he passed the examination. ...so nobody came. ...however, she did not tell anybody.*
Each row writes a beginning for each. Three minutes.
Read them out. The interest is in how differently the rows completed the same one, and in whether *although* and *however* were used correctly - they usually are not.
Fix the *although* and *however* errors together, since those two are worth more marks at O/L than the other two.
blocks.variation: Harder: the same result must be given two different causes, one using *because* and one using *although*.
blocks.bigClass: Four prompts, five rows, twenty sentences to read - which is about two minutes, the right length. Any more prompts and the reading round outlasts the writing.

blocks.name: Rewrite it politely
blocks.language: Softening: modals, questions instead of commands
steps: Board five blunt sentences: *Give me your book. I want leave tomorrow. Your answer is wrong. Send the form. Come here.*
Every pupil rewrites all five so that they could be said to a principal.
Pairs compare and choose the politer version of each, giving a reason.
Board the class's best five and keep them up for the rest of the week.
blocks.variation: Harder: rewrite them a third way, for a friend, so the class sees all three registers side by side.
blocks.bigClass: Individual writing keeps it silent, and the pair comparison is where the judgement is trained. Leaving the five best on the board for a week is the part that actually changes their writing.

items.q: Which conditional should I spend the most time on?
a: The first, by a distance. It is the one a pupil will actually use - *if it rains, we will not go* - and it is the one that appears most in examination papers. The second conditional is worth a game because pupils enjoy it, and the third is worth knowing exists. Do not spend three weeks on all three.

items.q: Is the passive worth teaching at this level?
a: Yes, but for reading before writing. Pupils meet the passive constantly in notices, instructions and textbooks - *entries must be submitted by Friday* - and not understanding it costs them marks in comprehension. The two passive games below are built around recognising and using it for a reason, not transforming sentences.

items.q: My pupils write the way they message each other.
a: That is not laziness, it is the only written English most of them use daily. The fix is not to forbid it but to make the comparison explicit and frequent: the same message written two ways, side by side, until they can feel the difference. The formal-or-friendly game does exactly that in seven minutes.

pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 10, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.
pages.keywords: grade 10 english games, english classroom games grade 10, esl games grade 10, english language games for large classes, no preparation english games

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 10 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: the writing formats the O/L paper asks for - notices, letters, dialogues, forms - done fast and to a word limit.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 10 class needs from a game
text: From Grade 10 a game has to justify itself against revision, and the honest way to do that is to make it produce what the paper produces. Every game below ends with a notice, a letter, a dialogue, a form or a paragraph of the kind the Ordinary Level asks for.

The other thing these are built around is speed. The commonest reason for lost marks in the writing section is not poor English but an unfinished answer, and a pupil who has written forty notices in a term under a clock does not run out of time in November.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: The letter race
blocks.language: The formal letter: address, salutation, body, closing
steps: Give a situation that needs a formal letter: asking the principal for a certificate, writing to a bookshop about a wrong order.
Eight minutes on the clock, visible. Everybody writes the whole letter, format included.
Stop exactly on time even if nobody has finished, because that is the lesson.
Pairs swap and mark against four things on the board: the format, whether every part of the task was answered, the length, and the register. Marks out of eight.
blocks.variation: Harder: six minutes instead of eight, once the class can finish in eight.
blocks.bigClass: Everything is individual and silent until the swap, so size does not matter. The visible clock is essential - a spoken time limit does not produce the same urgency.

blocks.name: Notice in fifty words
blocks.language: The notice: what, when, where, who to contact, and brevity
steps: Give a situation. Four minutes to write a notice of no more than fifty words.
Swap with the pair behind. The marking pair counts the words first - over the limit loses marks before anything else is read, exactly as on the paper.
They then check the four required items and circle anything unnecessary.
Board the shortest notice that still contains everything, and read it out.
blocks.variation: Harder: thirty-five words, which forces every article and adjective to justify itself.
blocks.bigClass: Counting the words first is what makes this stick. Pupils who have lost marks to a word count in a game stop ignoring it on the paper.

blocks.name: The dialogue builder
blocks.language: Completing a dialogue: question forms, short answers, natural replies
steps: Board a six-line dialogue with three lines missing - a pupil asking a teacher about a school trip, say.
Pairs write the missing lines. Three minutes.
Two or three pairs read their whole dialogue aloud, both parts.
The class judges which filled lines actually fit what comes after them - the commonest O/L error here is a line that makes sense alone but not in the conversation.
blocks.variation: Harder: the last line is fixed and unusual, so the middle must be steered towards it.
blocks.bigClass: Reading aloud in pairs is the check: a line that does not fit sounds wrong immediately, which is far more convincing to a class than being told.

blocks.name: Mark my answer
blocks.prep: A sample answer on the board, written by you
blocks.language: The marking criteria themselves
steps: Board a complete answer to a past question - one you have written, at about the level of a middling pupil, with two or three typical faults in it.
Give the class the criteria, and let pairs mark it out of ten with a reason for each mark lost.
Collect the marks. The spread will be wide, which is itself worth discussing.
Then give your own mark and explain it. Pupils who marked far above or below yours have learned the most.
blocks.variation: Two answers of different quality, and the class must place them in order and say what separates them.
blocks.bigClass: One answer on the board, forty-five markers. This is the single most useful game on this page, and it needs no materials at all.

blocks.name: Fill the form
blocks.prep: A blank form sketched on the board
blocks.language: Form-filling conventions: capitals, dates, no full sentences
steps: Draw a simple form on the board - an application for a library card, a competition entry - with eight or nine fields.
Everybody copies and fills it. Four minutes.
Then give three awkward extras aloud: a field they must leave blank, a date that must be written in a particular way, a box that needs a tick rather than a word.
Pairs check each other for the commonest faults: sentences where a phrase is wanted, and a date written three different ways in one form.
blocks.variation: Harder: one field asks for something in fewer than ten words, which is where most marks are lost on a form question.
blocks.bigClass: Copying the form takes two of the six minutes, which is time well spent: copying a layout accurately is itself a marked skill.

blocks.name: Picture to paragraph
blocks.language: Describing and interpreting: present continuous, there is/are, and inference
steps: Everybody writes six sentences about a picture: three saying what is there, and three saying what they think is happening or about to happen.
The second three are the hard ones and the ones the paper rewards.
Around the rows, each pupil reads one inference sentence only.
The class decides which inferences the picture actually supports, which is exactly the judgement the comprehension section tests.
blocks.variation: Harder: no sentence may begin with *there is* or *there are*.
blocks.bigClass: Everybody writes six, everybody reads one. The ban on *there is* in the variation is worth using early, because half the class will otherwise write all six that way.

blocks.name: The invitation and the reply
blocks.language: Invitations, acceptances and refusals, formal and informal
steps: One pupil in each pair writes an invitation - to a school concert, a wedding, a sports meet - in the format on the board. Three minutes.
They pass it to their partner, who writes the reply. Half the class should be told privately to refuse, and to give a reason.
Refusing politely is much harder than accepting, and that is why half the class must do it.
Read two acceptances and two refusals, and ask the class which refusal was the least awkward.
blocks.variation: Harder: the refusal must offer an alternative, which needs a conditional.
blocks.bigClass: Passing within a pair means no movement. Make sure the refusals are distributed across the room rather than to one side, so both kinds get read out from different rows.

blocks.name: Spot the lost marks
blocks.prep: A short answer on the board with four faults in it
blocks.language: The four commonest ways marks are lost in the writing section
steps: Board a short answer containing exactly four faults: one part of the task not answered, one register error, one over-long section, one format slip. Do not say what kind they are.
Rows find all four. Three minutes.
Take them one at a time. The part-not-answered is the one rows miss most often, and it is the one that costs the most on the paper.
Rewrite the weakest sentence together as a class.
blocks.variation: Put five faults in and tell them there are four, so they must decide which they are most confident about.
blocks.bigClass: One answer on the board, nine rows hunting. Say the number of faults but not their kinds - knowing there are four and having found three is what makes a class read carefully.

items.q: Is there time for games in Grade 10?
a: There is time for whatever produces the most writing per minute, and a well-run game usually beats a revision worksheet on that measure. Judge each one by what is on the page at the end. If nothing is, it did not belong in Grade 10.

items.q: My pupils know the formats but still lose marks.
a: Almost always for one of three things: not answering all parts of the question, running out of time, or ignoring the word limit. All three are habits rather than knowledge, and habits are what a repeated timed game builds. The marking game below is the fastest way to show them where the marks actually go.

items.q: Should I mark everything they produce in these?
a: No, and you could not. Most of these end with pupils marking each other against the criteria, which teaches more than your red pen does, because a pupil who has marked four notices knows what a notice needs. Collect one set a fortnight and mark that properly.

pages.title: Grade 11 English Classroom Games
pages.description: Eight English classroom games for Grade 11, each with the language it practises, the time it takes and what to do in a class of forty-five. No equipment needed.
pages.keywords: grade 11 english games, english classroom games grade 11, esl games grade 11, english language games for large classes, no preparation english games

hero.text: Eight games for a Grade 11 class, each tied to what this grade is actually learning: the O/L paper itself - each section done against a clock, marked against the criteria, and repaired.

blocks.heading: What a Grade 11 class needs from a game
text: In the examination year a game has to be defensible in November, so every one of these is a piece of the Ordinary Level paper done under a clock. They are still games, with a score and a reason to hurry, but nothing here is played for its own sake.

The clock is the design. Marks at O/L are lost to unfinished answers far more often than to poor English, and no amount of explaining fixes that - only doing it repeatedly, against a visible timer, until finishing in the time becomes ordinary.

blocks.title: Eight games, no equipment
text: None of these needs a photocopier, a projector or a set of cards. Every one says what to do when the class has forty-five pupils in it, because that is the class most teachers reading this have.

blocks.name: Beat the clock
blocks.prep: One writing question from a past paper
blocks.language: Whichever section you are working on
steps: Put the real time allowance for that question on the board as a countdown, and take two minutes off it.
Everybody writes. No questions once it starts.
Stop dead on time. Ask for a show of hands: finished, nearly finished, not finished.
Repeat the same question type next week at the real allowance, and compare the hands. The improvement is visible within a month.
blocks.variation: Once the class can finish comfortably, cut another minute rather than lengthening the question.
blocks.bigClass: Silent and individual, so class size is irrelevant. The show of hands is the whole feedback mechanism and it costs ten seconds.

blocks.name: The examiner's eye
blocks.prep: Two answers to the same question, written by you at different levels
blocks.language: The marking criteria
steps: Board or read out two answers to the same question - one worth about half marks, one worth most of them. Do not say which is which.
Pairs decide which is better and list three specific things that separate them. Not *better English* - three things.
Collect the reasons and board them. The list the class produces is the marking criteria in their own words, which they will remember.
Keep that list on the wall for the rest of the year.
blocks.variation: Make the two answers closer in quality each time you use it.
blocks.bigClass: The list on the wall is what makes this worth the period. A criteria list the class wrote themselves gets read; one you hand out does not.

blocks.name: The rewrite challenge
blocks.prep: One weak paragraph on the board
blocks.language: Repairing rather than producing
steps: Board a weak paragraph - genuinely weak, with repetition, short choppy sentences and one good idea buried in it.
Each row rewrites it. Five minutes, one sheet passed along.
Rows read their versions. The class votes, and must say what made the winner better.
Then ask what the original's one good idea was, and whether every version kept it. Usually one row has lost it, which is worth a minute.
blocks.variation: Harder: the rewrite must be shorter than the original while keeping everything that mattered.
blocks.bigClass: The buried good idea is the design. It stops the game being about polish and makes it about reading the original properly first.

blocks.name: Twenty marks in ten minutes
blocks.language: Reading the question and allocating effort
steps: Give the rows a section of a past paper and its mark allocation, but do not let them start writing.
Two minutes: each row plans how many minutes it would spend on each question and why. That is the whole first half of the game.
Compare the plans. Rows almost always over-allocate to the question they like and under-allocate to the one worth the most marks.
Then write for the remaining time according to the class's agreed plan.
blocks.variation: Include a question worth very few marks that looks time-consuming, and see which rows spot it.
blocks.bigClass: The planning half is the lesson and it is free. Most classes have never once been asked to decide where the time should go before writing.

blocks.name: The dialogue under time
blocks.language: Completing a dialogue at speed
steps: Board a dialogue with four gaps and give four minutes.
Pairs fill it, then read it aloud to the pair behind them, both parts.
The listening pair says which line sounded wrong. Something always does, and hearing it is faster than analysing it.
Fix the two commonest wrong lines with the whole class.
blocks.variation: Harder: one gap is the last line, which has to close the conversation - the hardest of the four.
blocks.bigClass: Reading to the pair behind means twenty-two dialogues are heard and judged in two minutes, which no whole-class reading round could achieve.

blocks.name: Spot the lost marks, again
blocks.prep: A complete answer with faults, from the class's own work, anonymised
blocks.language: Where marks actually go
steps: Take a real answer from the class's books - no name, and rewritten in your hand so it cannot be recognised.
Rows find every place a mark would be lost and say why.
Total the losses. The class's total is almost always higher than the real one, which is worth discussing: pupils over-punish grammar and under-punish an unanswered part.
Give the real mark and where it actually went.
blocks.variation: Use an answer that is strong in English but misses half the task, which is the most instructive kind.
blocks.bigClass: Anonymising properly matters more in a large class, not less - rewrite it in your own hand, and never use an answer whose writer could be guessed from its content.

blocks.name: The essay plan race
blocks.language: Planning: thesis, three points, conclusion
steps: Give three titles. Everybody plans all three in six minutes - plans only, four lines each, no prose.
The point is that planning an essay should take three minutes, not fifteen, and most pupils have never timed it.
Take one title and compare four plans aloud. Ask which plan would produce the best essay, not which sounds cleverest.
Then they write the essay from the winning plan, for homework or next period.
blocks.variation: Harder: one of the three titles should be awkward and unfamiliar, since that is the one that appears in November.
blocks.bigClass: Silent and individual. Comparing four plans aloud takes three minutes and shows the class that a good plan is short, which is the thing they least believe.

blocks.name: The last five minutes
blocks.language: Checking: tense, agreement, full stops, the word count
steps: Take an answer the class wrote earlier in the week. Give them five minutes and a checking list of four items on the board.
They check their own first, alone, for two minutes, then swap and check a partner's for three.
Count how many errors each pupil found in their own work, and how many their partner found in it. The second number is always larger.
That gap is the lesson: you cannot see your own mistakes well, which is why the checking list exists.
blocks.variation: Use the four errors the class actually makes most, taken from your own marking, and change the list each month.
blocks.bigClass: Five minutes, no materials, and it can be done at the end of any period with anything they have written. The comparison of the two numbers is what makes them believe in checking at all.

items.q: We have no time for anything but past papers.
a: Then use these on the past papers you are already doing. Most of them are ways of working through a paper rather than alternatives to one: marking each other's answers, repairing a weak paragraph, finding where the marks went. The paper is still the material; what changes is what the class does with it.

items.q: My class panics about the time.
a: Panic comes from not knowing how long an answer takes, and the only cure is having done it often enough to know. Put the clock where everybody can see it and stop exactly on time every single occasion, including when they are close. A class that has been stopped forty times stops being frightened of it.

items.q: Is it worth letting pupils mark each other?
a: It is the most valuable thing on this page. A pupil who has marked six answers against the criteria understands where marks come from in a way that no amount of having their own work marked achieves. Your marking tells them about their answer; marking six tells them about the paper.

items.q: What about the pupils who have already given up?
a: Score by row so they are contributing to something, and give them the marking and checking roles, which are less exposed than producing. A pupil who will not write a letter will often happily find four faults in somebody else's, and that is real engagement with the paper.
